# Supaṇṇa Saṁyutta (SN 30)

**ID:** SN 30

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Supaṇṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 30) is the thirtieth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, consisting of four suttas delivered at Sāvatthī [Bodhi 2003]. It forms the second of four closely associated collections (SN 29–32) that describe classes of semi-celestial beings traditionally viewed as mythological—*nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, *gandhabbas*, and cloud devas (*valāhakas*)—and the karmic courses of action leading to rebirth in their company [Bodhi 2003]. *Supaṇṇas* (also identified with *garuḍas* or described as harpies) are powerful winged bird-spirits known in Indian mythology as the natural antagonists of *nāgas* [Hazra 1994]. According to the collection's commentary, *supaṇṇas* are only able to seize *nāgas* of an inferior or equal grade, but cannot overcome those of a higher class [Bodhi 2003_x].

The text outlines the four modes of generation (*yoni*) for *supaṇṇas*: egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), womb-born (*jalābuja*), moisture-born (*saṁsedaja*), and spontaneously born (*opapātika*) [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994]. Across these suttas, the Buddha explains the karmic mechanisms of rebirth in each grade, detailing how rebirth can arise either merely through admiring the beings and forming an aspiration, or through cultivating that resolve alongside the practice of generosity, such as giving gifts of food and requisites to ascetics [Bodhi 2003; Langer 2007].
